latency.def: How long one request takes, from the moment it's sent to the moment the answer arrives. Usually measured in milliseconds.

throughput.def: How many requests (or how much data) a system handles per second. A system can have high throughput and still be slow for each request.

percentile.def: p99 is the time that 99% of requests beat; only the slowest 1% take longer. p50 is the median. Percentiles show the slow requests that averages hide.

availability.def: The share of time (or of requests) a system works and answers correctly, often quoted in 'nines': 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year.

durability.def: The promise that data the system has accepted won't be lost later, even when disks or machines fail.

eventual-consistency.def: Copies of the data may briefly disagree after a write, but catch up if no new writes arrive. Readers can see slightly old data for a moment.

redundancy.def: Keeping spare copies of a component or of data, so that when one fails another can take over.

error-budget.def: The failures a service is allowed under its availability target. 99.9% leaves a 0.1% budget; teams spend it on shipping changes and slow down when it runs out.

read-heavy.def: A system where reads far outnumber writes, like a link shortener that's opened far more often than links are created. Designs for these focus on making reads cheap.

redirect.def: A response that tells the browser to go to a different URL instead. 301 means 'moved for good' (browsers remember it); 302 means 'go there this time'.

cache.def: A fast store, usually in memory, that keeps copies of data that's read often, so it doesn't have to be fetched from the slower original every time.

load-balancer.def: A component that receives incoming requests and spreads them across several servers, skipping any that are unhealthy.

replica.def: A copy of a database kept up to date from the main one. Replicas can serve reads and take over if the main copy fails.

sharding.def: Splitting one large dataset across several databases (shards), each holding part of the data, so no single machine has to store or serve all of it.

message-queue.def: A buffer between programs: one side drops messages in, the other takes them out and processes them later, at its own pace.

cdn.def: Content delivery network: servers spread around the world that keep copies of files close to users, so they load faster.

ssd.def: Solid-state drive: storage built from memory chips instead of spinning platters. Much faster than a hard disk, much slower than RAM.

api.def: The set of requests a program accepts from other programs, and what it sends back. For a web service, usually its URLs and their inputs and outputs.

uuid.def: A 128-bit random-looking ID, usually written as 36 characters, that can be generated anywhere without checking with anyone and still be unique.

single-point-of-failure.def: One part whose failure takes the whole system down with it, because nothing else can do its job.

vertical-scaling.def: Handling more load by moving to a bigger machine: more CPU, memory or faster disks. No code changes, but there's a ceiling.

horizontal-scaling.def: Handling more load by adding more machines and spreading the work across them.

failover.def: Switching to a standby copy when the main one fails, so the system keeps working.

stateless.def: A server that keeps nothing between requests that another server would need, so any copy can handle any request.

sticky-session.def: A load balancer setting that always sends the same user to the same server. A workaround for servers that keep state.

health-check.def: A small request a load balancer sends to each server every few seconds. Servers that fail it stop getting traffic.

replication-lag.def: The delay between a write on the primary database and a replica applying it. During it, the replica returns old data.

hit-rate.def: The share of reads a cache answers itself. The rest (misses) go to the slower store behind it.

cache-aside.def: The app checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and stores the answer in the cache for next time.

ttl.def: Time to live: how long a cached copy may be kept before it expires and has to be fetched again.

origin.def: The servers that hold the real content behind a CDN. Edge servers fetch from the origin when they don't have a copy.

edge-server.def: One of a CDN's servers, placed close to users, that keeps copies of content so requests don't have to travel to the origin.

worker.def: A background program that takes jobs off a queue and does them, away from the requests users are waiting on.

at-least-once.def: A queue guarantee that every message is delivered, possibly more than once. Consumers must be safe to run twice.

idempotent.def: Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, like setting a value rather than adding to it.

dead-letter-queue.def: A side queue for messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected without blocking the rest.

dns.def: The internet's phone book: it turns a name like snip.link into the IP address of a server, with answers cached for a set time (the TTL).

tls.def: The encryption layer under HTTPS. A TLS handshake proves the server's identity with a certificate and agrees keys before any data is sent.

round-trip.def: A message going to another machine and the reply coming back. Its time depends mostly on distance: about 0.5 ms inside a datacenter, 100 ms or more across an ocean.

tcp.def: The transport protocol most of the web uses: a handshake first, then every byte delivered reliably and in order.

udp.def: A transport protocol that sends packets with no handshake, no resending and no ordering. Used for DNS, video calls, games and QUIC.

head-of-line-blocking.def: When one delayed or lost item holds up everything queued behind it, even items that are ready.

quic.def: A transport protocol built on UDP, with encryption and independent streams built in. HTTP/3 runs on it.

rest.def: An API style built on resources with URLs and HTTP's own methods (GET, POST, DELETE…) and status codes.

grpc.def: A framework for calling functions on remote servers, with a typed schema, generated client code and compact binary messages over HTTP/2.

graphql.def: An API style with one endpoint and a typed schema, where the client writes a query naming exactly the fields it wants.

cursor-pagination.def: Paging through a list by passing back a token that marks where the last page ended, instead of a page number or offset.

websocket.def: A long-lived, two-way connection between browser and server, started as an HTTP request and upgraded.

sse.def: A one-way stream of events from server to browser over a single long-lived HTTP response, with automatic reconnect.

pub-sub.def: Publish/subscribe messaging: senders publish to a topic, and every subscriber to that topic gets a copy.

layer-4.def: Balancing connections by IP address and port, without reading the requests inside them.

layer-7.def: Balancing individual HTTP requests, which the balancer reads, so it can route by path, host or header.

draining.def: Taking a server out of rotation gently: no new requests, while the ones in progress are allowed to finish.

reverse-proxy.def: A server that clients talk to as if it were the site, which passes requests on to the real servers behind it.

api-gateway.def: A reverse proxy in front of an API's services that handles authentication, rate limits and routing in one place.

service-mesh.def: A proxy next to every service instance (a sidecar) that handles discovery, retries, timeouts, encryption and metrics for calls between services.

backoff.def: Waiting longer after each failed attempt before retrying: say 100 ms, then 200, then 400, up to a cap.

jitter.def: Randomness added to retry delays so that many clients don't all retry at the same moment.

circuit-breaker.def: A switch around calls to a dependency that, after many failures, fails calls immediately for a while instead of trying them.

idempotency-key.def: A unique value a client sends with a request so that retries of the same operation can be recognised and not repeated.

load-shedding.def: Rejecting some requests quickly when a server is overloaded, so that it can serve the rest within their deadlines.

backpressure.def: A full queue or busy component pushing back on whoever is sending it work, so they slow down instead of piling up more.

goodput.def: The requests a system answers successfully and in time for the client to use. Overloaded systems can have high throughput and near-zero goodput.

tail-latency.def: The latency of the slowest requests, such as the p99 or p99.9. In large systems it shapes what most users feel.

hedged-request.def: Sending a second copy of a slow request to another server and using whichever answer comes first.

fan-out.def: One request or message spreading to many servers or recipients. A request that fans out waits for the slowest of them.

rate-limit.def: A cap on how many requests a caller may make in a period. Requests over it are rejected, usually with HTTP 429.

primary-key.def: The column or columns that uniquely identify each row in a table. The database guarantees no two rows share one.

foreign-key.def: A column that refers to another table's primary key. The database rejects values that don't point at a real row.

normalisation.def: Structuring tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place, and other tables refer to it by key.

denormalisation.def: Deliberately storing a fact (often a derived one, like a count) in a second place so that a frequent read is cheap.

index.def: A sorted copy of one or more columns, with pointers to rows, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.

b-tree.def: The tree structure most database indexes use: sorted keys packed hundreds to a page, a few levels deep even for billions of rows.

full-table-scan.def: Reading every row of a table to answer a query, because no index can narrow it down.

covering-index.def: An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database can answer from the index without reading the table.

query-plan.def: The database's chosen way of running a query: which indexes, which order, which join method. EXPLAIN shows it.

transaction.def: A group of database changes that succeed or fail together, isolated from other transactions running at the same time.

acid.def: Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable: the guarantees a database transaction gives.

isolation-level.def: How much concurrent transactions are shielded from each other: read committed, snapshot (repeatable read), serializable.

write-skew.def: Two transactions read the same data, each decide it's safe to proceed, and write different rows that together break a rule.

snapshot-isolation.def: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database taken when it started. Prevents most anomalies, but not write skew.

serializable.def: The strictest isolation level: transactions behave as if they ran one at a time. Some are aborted and must be retried.

mvcc.def: Multi-version concurrency control: keeping several versions of each row so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers.

vacuum.def: Postgres's background cleanup that removes dead row versions left behind by updates and deletes.

wal.def: An append-only log of every change, flushed to disk before a commit is acknowledged. Replayed after crashes and shipped to replicas.

checkpoint.def: A point at which all changes so far have been written to the data files, so crash recovery only replays the log after it.

point-in-time-recovery.def: Restoring a base backup and replaying archived write-ahead log up to a chosen moment, such as just before a bad delete.

leader.def: The one database server in a replicated group that accepts writes and sends its log to the followers.

synchronous-replication.def: The leader waits for followers to confirm a write before acknowledging it, so failover loses nothing, at the cost of latency.

split-brain.def: Two servers both believing they're the leader and accepting writes, so the data diverges.

fencing.def: Making sure an old leader can no longer accept writes once a new one has been promoted.

connection-pooler.def: A proxy like PgBouncer that lets many application connections share a small number of real database connections.

partitioning.def: Splitting one big table into pieces by a key, usually time, inside one database, so queries and deletes touch only the pieces they need.

vertical-partitioning.def: Moving groups of tables onto their own databases, so each database serves fewer tables and less load.

expand-contract.def: Changing a schema in compatible steps: add the new shape, write both, backfill, switch reads and writes, then remove the old.

backfill.def: Filling a new column or table with values for existing rows, usually in small batches while the system runs.

partition-key.def: The value a distributed database hashes to decide which machine holds a row. Queries by it are fast; queries across it are not.

columnar-store.def: A database that stores each column separately and compressed, making scans and aggregates over billions of rows fast.

source-of-truth.def: The one store whose copy of some data is authoritative. Caches, indexes and other copies are derived from it.

shard-key.def: The column (or columns) used to decide which shard a row lives on. Queries that include it go to one shard; queries without it must ask them all.

scatter-gather.def: Sending one query to every shard and merging their answers. Needed when a query doesn't include the shard key, and only as fast as the slowest shard.

logical-shard.def: One of a fixed, large number of data partitions, several of which live on each machine. Keys map to logical shards permanently; growing means moving whole logical shards to new machines.

hot-partition.def: A shard or partition receiving far more traffic than the others, usually because of one very popular key, one very big tenant, or a key that follows time.

hot-key.def: A single key, such as a viral link or a celebrity's profile, that gets a large share of all requests. Hashing can't spread it, because every request for it goes to the same place.

split-counter.def: One logical counter stored as several rows, each write updating one at random and reads summing them, so a hot counter's writes spread out.

request-coalescing.def: Letting one request fetch a value while identical requests arriving at the same time wait for its answer, so a database is queried once instead of many times.

consistent-hashing.def: Placing servers and keys on the same hash ring and giving each key to the next server clockwise, so adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys.

virtual-node.def: One of many positions a server takes on a consistent hashing ring. Hundreds per server even out the load and spread a failed server's keys across the rest.

rendezvous-hashing.def: Choosing a server for a key by scoring every server with a hash of the key and server together and picking the highest. Moves few keys on change, with no ring to store.

rebalancing.def: Moving data between machines so load is even again after machines are added, removed or fill up, ideally while the system keeps serving.

cutover.def: The moment traffic switches from the old copy of some data to the new one, usually after a brief pause to let the last changes replicate.

dark-read.def: Reading the same data from both an old and a new system and comparing the results, while still serving only the old one. Used to verify a migration before switching.

logical-replication.def: Copying changes as rows inserted, updated or deleted, rather than as raw disk pages, so they can be applied to a database with a different layout or version.

snowflake-id.def: A 64-bit ID made of a millisecond timestamp, a machine number and a sequence, so each machine can generate unique, roughly time-ordered IDs on its own.

uuidv7.def: A UUID whose first 48 bits are a millisecond timestamp and the rest random, so new IDs sort after old ones and insert at one end of an index.

ticket-server.def: A small database whose only job is handing out the next number from a counter, giving a sharded system unique IDs.

base62.def: Writing numbers using 62 characters: the digits and the upper and lower case letters. Seven base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion values.

clock-skew.def: The difference between two machines' clocks at the same instant. Timestamps from different machines can't order events closer together than the skew.

ntp.def: Network Time Protocol: how servers keep their clocks close to the right time by checking against time servers, typically to within a few milliseconds.

monotonic-clock.def: A clock that only ever moves forward, used to measure how much time has passed. Unlike the time of day, it never jumps backwards when corrected.

last-write-wins.def: Resolving conflicting updates by keeping the one with the latest timestamp. Simple, but a skewed clock can make it silently discard the newer write.

lamport-clock.def: A counter each machine increments on every event and sends with every message, jumping ahead when it receives a larger one, so causes are always ordered before their effects.

keyset-pagination.def: Fetching the next page as the rows after the last one seen (by its sort key), instead of skipping a count of rows. Every page costs the same and pages don't drift.

bloom-filter.def: A compact bit array that answers "definitely not in the set" or "probably in it", using a few bits per item. It never misses an added item, but sometimes says maybe for one it never saw.

false-positive.def: A wrong "yes": a check that says something is present, or true, when it isn't.

in-process-cache.def: A cache kept in an app server's own memory. The fastest kind, with no network hop, but each server has its own copy, which starts empty after a deploy.

read-through.def: A caching pattern where the app only asks the cache, and the cache itself loads missing entries from the database.

write-through.def: A caching pattern where every write goes to the database and the cache together, so the cache is always up to date and warm.

write-behind.def: A caching pattern where writes go to the cache first and are copied to the database later, in batches. Fast, but unflushed writes are lost if the cache dies. Also called write-back.

eviction-policy.def: The rule a full cache uses to choose which entry to remove to make room, such as least recently used (LRU) or least frequently used (LFU).

lru.def: Least recently used: an eviction policy that removes the entry that hasn't been read for the longest time.

lfu.def: Least frequently used: an eviction policy that removes the entry read the fewest times.

cache-invalidation.def: Removing or replacing cached copies when the original data changes, so readers stop seeing the old value.

change-data-capture.def: Reading a database's log of committed changes and passing each change on to other systems, such as caches, search indexes or analytics.

cache-stampede.def: Many requests missing the same cache entry at once (often when a popular entry expires) and all querying the database for it together. Also called a thundering herd.

lease.def: A right granted for a limited time that lapses unless renewed: a lock or leadership that expires if its holder stops renewing it, or, in a cache, a token making one client responsible for refilling a key.

soft-ttl.def: An earlier expiry after which a cached value is stale but still served while it's refreshed in the background. A hard TTL marks when it can't be used at all.

hash-slot.def: One of a fixed number of partitions a cluster divides its keys into. Redis Cluster uses 16,384; nodes own ranges of slots, and resharding moves whole slots.

cache-key.def: What a cache stores a response under. For a CDN it's usually the full URL, so anything in it that doesn't change the answer, such as tracking parameters, splits one object into many entries.

purge.def: Telling a CDN to drop cached copies before they expire, by URL or by tag.

surrogate-key.def: A tag attached to a cached response so that one purge can clear every object carrying it, such as all of one owner's links.

tiered-caching.def: Arranging a CDN's locations in tiers, so edges that miss ask an upper-tier location and only the upper tier asks the origin.

stale-while-revalidate.def: A Cache-Control setting that lets a cache serve an expired response for a set time while it fetches a fresh one in the background.

littles-law.def: The average number of items waiting equals the arrival rate times the average time each waits. A backlog divided by the drain rate tells you how late the work is.

event-log.def: An append-only, ordered sequence of events that keeps them after they're read, so many readers can each go through it at their own pace and replay it. Kafka is the best-known example.

consumer-offset.def: A reader's position in a log partition: the number of the next event it will process. Saving it records progress.

visibility-timeout.def: How long a queue hides a message after handing it to a worker. If the worker doesn't acknowledge it in time, the message reappears for another worker.

at-most-once.def: A delivery guarantee where a message may be lost but is never processed twice.

exactly-once.def: Processing where each message's effect happens once. In practice it's at-least-once delivery plus consumers that recognise and skip repeats.

consumer-group.def: A set of readers that share a log topic's partitions, each partition read by one member at a time. Separate groups each read every event.

rebalance.def: Reassigning a log's partitions among a consumer group's members when one joins, leaves or fails.

skip-locked.def: A Postgres locking option that makes a query skip rows other transactions have locked, so many workers can claim different jobs from one table without waiting.

dual-write.def: Writing the same change to two systems, such as a database and a message broker, one after the other. A crash between them leaves the two disagreeing.

transactional-outbox.def: Writing an event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the change it describes, so a separate relay can publish it afterwards. Both happen, or neither.

logical-decoding.def: A Postgres feature that turns the write-ahead log into a stream of row changes, which change data capture tools read.

saga.def: A long process split into steps that each commit on their own, with a compensating step for each, run in reverse if a later step fails.

compensating-transaction.def: A new action that undoes the business effect of an earlier step, such as a refund for a charge. Unlike a rollback, both remain visible.

orchestration.def: Coordinating a multi-step process from one component that calls each service in turn and handles failures, rather than having services react to each other's events (choreography).

choreography.def: Coordinating a multi-step process without a central controller: each service reacts to events and publishes its own.

fan-out-on-write.def: Copying a new item into every recipient's precomputed list when it's created, so reading a list is cheap. Also called push.

fan-out-on-read.def: Building each recipient's list at read time by querying and merging sources, so writes are cheap. Also called pull.

partial-failure.def: Some parts of a distributed system failing while others keep working, so a request can succeed, fail, or end with an unknown outcome.

network-partition.def: A network fault that splits machines into groups that can't reach each other, while each group keeps running.

gray-failure.def: A component that's working badly rather than down, such as a slow node, so health checks pass while users suffer.

linearizable.def: The strongest single-object consistency: the system behaves as if there were one copy, and every read sees the latest completed write.

causal-consistency.def: A guarantee that changes which could have caused one another are seen in that order everywhere; unrelated changes may appear in any order.

read-your-writes.def: A guarantee that after you change something, your own later reads always see the change.

monotonic-reads.def: A guarantee that once you've seen a value, you never later see an older one.

cap-theorem.def: During a network partition, a distributed system can't be both linearizable and available to every request.

pacelc.def: An extension of CAP: during a Partition choose Availability or Consistency; Else choose Latency or Consistency.

quorum.def: The number of replicas that must respond for an operation to count, often a majority. With N copies, reads of R and writes of W overlap when R + W > N.

sloppy-quorum.def: Accepting a write on whichever nodes are reachable, not only the key's home replicas, to stay available; it weakens the read-write overlap.

hinted-handoff.def: A node accepting a write for an unreachable replica and passing it on when that replica returns.

read-repair.def: Fixing stale replicas during a read: when replicas disagree, the newest value is written back to the out-of-date ones.

anti-entropy.def: A background process that compares replicas and copies over whatever is missing or stale.

merkle-tree.def: A tree of hashes over ranges of data, letting two replicas find which ranges differ without comparing every item.

happened-before.def: The relation between events where one could have influenced the other: earlier on the same machine, or a message's send before its receipt. Events with no such link are concurrent.

vector-clock.def: A counter per node attached to each version of data. Comparing two vectors shows whether one version descends from the other or they were written concurrently.

hybrid-logical-clock.def: A timestamp that follows the physical clock but adds a logical counter, so it stays close to real time while still respecting cause and effect.

consensus.def: Getting a group of machines to agree on a value or a sequence of decisions, even when some fail; it needs a majority to make progress.

raft.def: A consensus algorithm designed to be understandable: a leader per term, elected by majority vote, replicates a log that commits once a majority has it.

leader-election.def: Choosing one instance out of several to be active, and replacing it when it fails, usually with a lease in a consensus store.

fencing-token.def: A number that increases each time a lock or leadership is granted. Writes carry it, and storage rejects any token older than one it has seen.

bulkhead.def: Giving each dependency its own pool of connections or threads, so one that hangs can't use up resources the others need.

gossip-protocol.def: Nodes periodically share what they know with a few random peers, so news reaches everyone in a number of rounds that grows with the logarithm of cluster size.

two-phase-commit.def: Committing across several databases: first each participant prepares and promises to commit, then the coordinator tells all to commit, or all to roll back.

tombstone.def: A record that marks a key as deleted. Append-only stores can't erase old data, so they write a tombstone that hides older values until compaction removes both.

compaction.def: Rewriting a store's files to keep only the latest live value of each key, removing overwritten and deleted data.

write-amplification.def: Bytes actually written to disk for each byte the application wrote, from page rewrites, logs and compaction.

read-amplification.def: Pages or files a storage engine reads to answer one lookup.

space-amplification.def: Disk space used for each byte of live data, from empty space in pages or old versions not yet compacted.

lsm-tree.def: Log-structured merge-tree: a storage engine that buffers writes in memory, flushes them as immutable sorted files, and merges those files in the background.

memtable.def: An LSM-tree's in-memory sorted buffer of recent writes, flushed to disk as a sorted file when full.

sstable.def: Sorted string table: an immutable file of key-value pairs sorted by key, with a small index and usually a Bloom filter.

object-storage.def: A store for whole, immutable files (objects) under keys in a flat namespace, such as Amazon S3, built to hold huge amounts of data cheaply.

multipart-upload.def: Uploading a large object in parts that are sent in parallel and retried independently, then combined.

presigned-url.def: A time-limited link that lets a browser upload or download one object directly from object storage, without passing through your servers.

erasure-coding.def: Splitting data into k pieces plus m parity pieces so that any k rebuild it, protecting against lost disks with far less storage than full copies.

reed-solomon.def: A family of erasure codes that can rebuild data from any k of its k + m pieces, used in storage systems, QR codes and CDs.

checksum.def: A short value computed from data and stored with it; recomputing it on read reveals whether the data changed.

silent-data-corruption.def: Wrong data returned with no error reported, from failing disks, memory, networks, software or CPUs.

scrubbing.def: Reading all stored data in the background to verify checksums and repair corruption before it's needed.

inverted-index.def: A map from each term to the sorted list of documents that contain it: the structure behind full-text search.

posting-list.def: The sorted list of document IDs (and often positions) stored for one term in an inverted index.

analyzer.def: The steps that turn text into index terms: splitting into words, lowercasing, removing stop words and stemming. Queries must use the same analysis.

stemming.def: Reducing words to a common root, so 'shoes' and 'shoe' match the same index term.

tf-idf.def: A relevance score: how often a term appears in a document (term frequency) times how rare the term is across all documents (inverse document frequency).

bm25.def: The default ranking function in Lucene-based search engines: TF-IDF with term frequency that saturates (k1) and normalization for document length (b).

scatter-gather-search.def: How a sharded search runs: every shard returns the IDs and scores of its own top results, the coordinator merges them, then fetches only the winning documents.

custom-routing.def: Choosing a document's shard from a value such as a tenant ID, so searches with the same value go to just that one shard.

embedding.def: A list of numbers produced by a model from text (or images) so that similar meanings give nearby vectors.

ann.def: Finding most of the closest vectors to a query without comparing it with every vector, trading a little recall for large speed-ups.

hnsw.def: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: an approximate nearest-neighbour index that searches a layered graph of vectors from coarse to fine.

hybrid-search.def: Running keyword (BM25) and vector search together and merging the results, so both exact terms and meaning count.

reciprocal-rank-fusion.def: Merging several ranked lists by giving each document 1 / (k + rank) per list and summing, so scores on different scales don't need comparing.

recall.def: The share of the truly relevant (or truly nearest) results that a search actually returns.

trie.def: A tree where each edge is a character and each node represents a prefix; used for prefix lookups like autocomplete.

debounce.def: Waiting for a short pause in user input before sending a request, so a burst of keystrokes becomes one request.

pre-aggregation.def: Summing events close to where they happen (say, per app server per second) and sending the totals, so far fewer writes reach storage.

sketch.def: A small data structure that answers a question about a large stream (distinct count, frequency, percentile) within a known error, using a tiny fraction of the memory.

event-time.def: When an event actually happened, recorded in the event itself, as opposed to processing time, when the system handled it.

watermark.def: A stream's estimate of how far event time has progressed: no more events older than it are expected, so windows before it can be emitted.

tumbling-window.def: A fixed-size, non-overlapping time window, such as each whole minute.

late-event.def: An event that arrives after the watermark has passed its timestamp, so its window may already have been emitted.

hyperloglog.def: A sketch that estimates how many distinct items it has seen, within about 1%, in a few kilobytes, and merges with other sketches by taking register maximums.

cardinality.def: The number of distinct items in a set, such as unique visitors.

count-min-sketch.def: A grid of counters with one hash per row that estimates how often any item occurred; it can over-count but never under-count.

heavy-hitter.def: An item that accounts for a large share of a stream, such as the most-clicked links in the last hour.

histogram.def: Counts of values in buckets (such as 0–5 ms, 5–10 ms). Histograms from many servers add up, so percentiles can be computed for the whole fleet.

t-digest.def: A mergeable sketch of a distribution that keeps small clusters near the extremes, giving accurate tail percentiles in little memory.

rollup.def: Pre-aggregated data at a coarser grain, such as one row per link per minute instead of one per click.

lambda-architecture.def: Running a batch path and a stream path side by side over the same events, with the batch path correcting the stream's results; it means writing the logic twice.

kappa-architecture.def: Keeping one stream processing path and recomputing results by replaying retained events through a new version of the same job.

gateway-server.def: A server whose job is holding clients' long-lived connections, authenticating them and writing messages out, while other services decide what to send.

connection-registry.def: A fast lookup from each connected user to the gateway server holding their connection, so messages can be routed to them.

reconnect-storm.def: Many clients reconnecting at the same moment, for example after a server restart, overloading the systems they reconnect to.

presence.def: Whether a user is online right now, usually inferred from recent heartbeats on their connection.

heartbeat.def: A small periodic message that says 'still here', so silence beyond a timeout can be treated as a failure or disconnection.

crdt.def: Conflict-free replicated data type: data whose copies can be updated independently and merged in any order to the same result.

home-timeline.def: A user's feed of recent posts from the accounts they follow.

social-graph.def: The network of relationships between users (follows, friends, likes), stored as edges between objects.

adjacency-list.def: Storing a graph as, for each node, the list of nodes it connects to; in a database, edge rows indexed by each end.

geohash.def: A string encoding of a location made by repeatedly halving longitude and latitude; points sharing a prefix lie in the same cell.

quadtree.def: A tree that splits a square into four whenever it holds too many points, so dense areas get smaller cells.

h3.def: Uber's hexagonal grid over the Earth, with 16 resolutions; every hexagon's neighbours are the same distance away.

s2.def: Google's library that divides the sphere into a hierarchy of cells ordered along Hilbert curves, each with a 64-bit ID.

nearest-neighbour.def: Finding the k points closest to a query point, such as the three nearest stores.

surge-pricing.def: Raising prices in an area where demand outstrips supply, to draw supply in and spread demand out.

collapse-key.def: A tag on push notifications so a newer one replaces an undelivered older one with the same key.

bearer-token.def: A credential that grants access to whoever presents it, with no further proof of identity, like a signed URL.

resumable-upload.def: An upload that can continue from where it stopped after a failure, instead of starting again.

image-variant.def: A version of an uploaded image at a particular size, format or quality, generated from the original.

srcset.def: An HTML attribute listing several versions of an image with their widths, so the browser can download the most suitable one.

transcoding.def: Re-encoding a video or audio file into a different format, resolution or bitrate.

adaptive-bitrate.def: Delivering video as short segments at several qualities, so the player can switch quality between segments as network conditions change.

bitrate-ladder.def: The set of resolutions and bitrates a video is encoded into for adaptive streaming.

hls.def: HTTP Live Streaming: a format where playlists list a video's quality variants and the short segment files of each.

keyframe.def: A video frame that can be decoded on its own, without earlier frames; segments must start on one for players to switch quality.

content-addressing.def: Naming data by a hash of its content, so identical data gets the same name and is stored once, and corruption is detectable.

content-defined-chunking.def: Splitting a file where a rolling hash of nearby bytes matches a pattern, so chunk boundaries survive insertions and deletions.

rolling-hash.def: A hash over a sliding window of bytes that can be updated cheaply as the window moves by one byte.

deduplication.def: Storing identical data only once, usually by recognising it from a hash of its content.

signed-url.def: A URL carrying an expiry and a cryptographic signature, which storage or a CDN honours without asking the application again.

signed-cookie.def: A signed credential in a cookie that authorises a set of paths, such as all of a video's segments, for a limited time.
